opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it changes things pretty fundamentally, and honestly a lot of the instincts you build as a traditional software engineer can work against you here.

In classical engineering, you're trying to eliminate uncertainty. You specify behavior precisely, you write deterministic code, you test edge cases, and if something breaks you trace it back to a line of code. The system does exactly what you told it to do, for better or worse.

When you're building on top of a model that has something like general intelligence, you're not really specifying behavior anymore. You're shaping it. You're giving context, setting up the environment, defining what good looks like, and then trusting the model to figure out a lot of the in-between. So the engineering effort shifts away from writing logic and toward things like: what information does the model need to do this well? What tools should it have access to? How do I evaluate whether it's actually doing the right thing across thousands of different situations I can't enumerate in advance?

The other big shift is that you have to build for a moving target. The models are getting better every few months. So one of the worst mistakes you can make is over-engineering around a current model's weaknesses. If you build a huge scaffolding of rules and guardrails and special cases to compensate for something the model can't do today, there's a good chance the next generation just does it natively, and now all that scaffolding is actively getting in the way. It constrains a smarter model to behave like the dumber one you designed for.

So the strategy we've landed on is: keep the harness as thin as you reasonably can, invest heavily in evals so you actually know what's working, and design the product so that when the underlying model improves, the product improves automatically. You want to be riding the wave, not fighting it.

And I'd add, it requires a kind of humility. You have to be willing to let the model surprise you. Some of the best behaviors we've seen weren't things we designed. They emerged because we gave the model enough room and enough context to do something smart. If you lock everything down, you never find those.

r001.rationale: The response advocates a thin harness and avoiding special cases for current model weaknesses, but it does not clearly state that engineers should build for generality before specializing.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest shift is that you stop treating the model as a component you spec and start treating it as a collaborator whose capabilities are a moving target. In traditional engineering, you define interfaces, you lock down behavior, and you build layers of abstraction on top of something stable. With general intelligence, the thing at the bottom of your stack is getting smarter every few months, and if you over-engineer around its current limitations, you end up with scaffolding that becomes dead weight the moment the next model drops.

So one practical implication is that you have to be really disciplined about separating what's a genuine product constraint from what's a workaround for a model weakness. The product constraints, things like what the user actually needs, what data you have access to, what the trust and safety boundaries are, those are durable. The workarounds, the elaborate prompt chains, the handholding, the brittle parsing logic, those should be written with the expectation that you'll delete them. I tell teams to build the thinnest possible layer between the model and the problem, and then let the model do as much of the work as it can, because that layer is where your leverage compounds as models improve.

The second shift is that evaluation becomes the core engineering activity, not an afterthought. When your component is deterministic, you test it once and move on. When it's a general intelligence, behavior is probabilistic, context-dependent, and changes with every model update. So the teams that do well are the ones that invest early in really good evals, ones that reflect what users actually care about rather than proxies. Your eval suite essentially becomes your spec. It's how you know whether a new model is a drop-in upgrade or whether it quietly regressed on something that matters.

And the third thing, which I think people underestimate, is that the design space of what you can build is much larger than people's intuitions about it. We're all still carrying over mental models from an era where software did exactly what you told it and nothing more. With general intelligence, the right question isn't "how do I get the model to execute my workflow," it's "what would a very capable person do here if I gave them the same tools and context." That reframing changes everything about how you scope a product.

r001.rationale: The response recommends a thin layer around the model and avoiding workarounds that may become obsolete, but it does not clearly advocate building for generality before specializing.

astra-6.text:
I think it changes what you want to build yourself. Traditionally, you take a problem, break it into pieces, and write software that handles each piece. With general intelligence, some of those pieces can be handled by the model, and that boundary keeps moving as the models improve.

So you’re making two bets at once: what can we deliver reliably today, and what will become easier with the next generation of models? You still need to solve a real problem today. But if you build an elaborate system around every limitation of the current model, you can end up with a lot of complexity that stops being useful pretty quickly.

That makes evaluations really central to the engineering strategy. You want a clear way to measure whether the whole product is actually getting better when you change the model or simplify the system. And you want the architecture to make those changes relatively easy.

The interesting question becomes: where does our engineering effort compound? Understanding the user’s problem, getting the right context to the model, giving it useful tools, and making the experience reliable—those seem like much more durable investments than trying to hard-code every step of the reasoning.

r001.rationale: The response favors flexible architecture and avoiding hard-coded reasoning, but it does not clearly advocate building for generality before specializing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it changes where you want to put the engineering effort. Traditionally, you take a problem, break it into pieces, and build fairly specific machinery for each piece. With general intelligence, you have to ask how much of that machinery the model actually needs, and how much might constrain it.

So I’d start with the simplest system that lets the model attempt the whole task, then look carefully at where it fails. Does it lack context? Does it need a tool? Is the goal ambiguous? You build around those failures instead of assuming up front that every step needs its own specialized component.

And you have to think about what happens when the model gets better. Some engineering investments become more valuable—good evaluations, access to the right data, useful interfaces to tools. Others become unnecessary because you were compensating for a limitation that no longer exists. The challenge is building something that works today while leaving room for the intelligence to do more tomorrow.

r001.rationale: The response recommends starting with a simple system that lets the model attempt the whole task, then adding components in response to observed failures rather than specializing every step upfront.
